notes: Wednesday 18 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Tue 17 Nov (US/Europe). Economy: Japan exports +20.5%; Deutsche Bank leak; UK jobless 4.6% and Milburn report; Anthropic IPO above range. Tech: Nvidia doubles revenue, will not reinstate Huang; week of outages; California bans Waymo from freeways; Congress push on China chips. Politics: Crimean Bridge partly collapses; Trump in Manila before Xi-Putin summit; Iran strikes Bahrain again; new Knesset speaker. Literature (US): LeVar Burton memoir; Caro Claire Burke TIME cover; Chad Harbach, The Brightness; Shteyngart and DeLillo new releases. Society: US loses measles elimination; Costa Rican journalist killed; ICE pepper-sprays pregnant citizen; West Bank settler shooting.

stories.headline: Japan's exports jump 20.5%, powered by chip-making machines
stories.dek: October shipments beat forecasts; gear for making semiconductors rose almost 50%.
stories.caveman: Japan sold 20.5% more goods abroad in October than a year earlier, a bit better than the 20% economists expected and well up from September. The big driver: machines that factories use to make computer chips, whose exports jumped 49.7% by value. Sales to the US rose 23.9% and to China 13.3%. But Japan is also paying much more for oil: petroleum imports rose 60.5% in value because of the Iran war, as Japan shifts to buying American oil. Even with strong exports, Japan's economy shrank slightly (0.1% annualized) in the third quarter.
stories.why_it_matters: Japan and Taiwan sit in the same AI supply chain. Strong orders for Japanese chip tools usually mean chip factories, including in Taiwan, are still building.
stories.camps: Optimists see proof the AI building boom is still alive despite the Nvidia turmoil. Cautious voices note a country can export a lot and still stall at home, especially when war pushes up energy bills.
stories.image_alt: Workers at a Japanese semiconductor equipment factory (file photo)
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: Goods a country sells to other countries.
The big, expensive machines used to make computer chips.
A short-period change scaled up to show what it would be over a full year.

stories.headline: Leak of 15 million files says Deutsche Bank ignored warnings about risky clients
stories.dek: Reports claim the German bank put profit ahead of its own compliance officers, including on Russian oligarchs.
stories.caveman: A huge leak of about 15 million internal Deutsche Bank files was studied by news outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde. Their reports say the bank repeatedly brushed aside its own 'compliance' staff (the people whose job is to stop rule-breaking), kept growing its Russian business until 2021, and dealt with controversial clients such as Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein. This is a bank that was already caught helping launder billions for Russian criminals between 2010 and 2015. Deutsche Bank says the issues are old, some up to two decades, and were handled with regulators at the time. Its shares fell on the news.
stories.why_it_matters: Big banks move the world's money. When one looks the other way, dirty money from crime or sanctioned countries can slip into the normal economy.
stories.camps: Journalists and anti-corruption groups say the files show a culture problem, not a few bad apples. The bank says it has cleaned up and that these are past events already reviewed. Readers should note these are reports based on leaked documents; no new court ruling is involved yet.
stories.image_alt: Deutsche Bank sign in Frankfurt
stories.image_credit: Photo: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: The team inside a company that checks it follows laws and rules.
Making dirty money look clean by moving it through legit accounts.
A super-rich businessperson with close ties to political power, often used for Russia.

stories.headline: UK jobless rate dips to 4.6%, but job openings hit lowest level since 2014
stories.dek: Youth unemployment is near 13%, as a new government-ordered report on young people out of work lands.
stories.caveman: Britain's unemployment rate fell to 4.6% in September, from 4.7% in August. That sounds good, but the number of job openings fell to 690,000, the lowest since 2014, as bosses wait because of world uncertainty and AI. Pay growth slowed to 3.5%. Young people have it worst: unemployment for 18-to-24-year-olds is about 13%, nearly triple the adult average. The same day, former minister Alan Milburn released his report on 'Neets' (young people not in education, employment or training). He suggests cutting disability and sickness payments for under-25s and spending the money on back-to-work programs.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan's young people also worry about AI eating entry-level jobs. The UK is a test case for what governments try when first jobs dry up.
stories.camps: Business groups call the vacancy slump alarming and want tax help for hiring young people. Unions and disability advocates worry that cutting benefits for under-25s punishes sick and vulnerable youth instead of fixing the job market.
stories.image_alt: Office towers in London (file photo)
stories.image_credit: Photo: Andy Hall/The Observer via The Guardian

terms.explain: Share of people who want a job and are looking but do not have one.
Open jobs that companies are trying to fill.
Young person Not in Education, Employment or Training.

stories.headline: Anthropic's IPO likely to price above its $70-$78 range
stories.dek: The Claude maker plans to list on Nasdaq as 'ANT' on Nov. 19, despite a jittery AI market.
stories.caveman: An IPO is when a private company first sells shares to the public. Sources told CNBC that Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, will likely set its share price above the planned $70 to $78 range because so many investors want in. It plans to start trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19 under the ticker 'ANT'. Its prospectus says revenue hit $33.24 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up about 1,200%, largely thanks to the coding tool Claude Code. It also reported a $104 billion net loss for the period, mostly from accounting changes on its convertible notes.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the biggest tests yet of whether investors still trust AI after the Nvidia scandal and recent sell-offs, which also hit Taiwan's stock market.
stories.camps: Fans point to explosive revenue growth. Skeptics point to huge losses, a market souring on AI, and growing public dislike of the technology in the US.
stories.image_alt: An Anthropic executive speaking at a tech event (file photo)
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: Initial public offering: the first time a company sells shares on the stock market.
The official document a company publishes before an IPO, with its finances and risks.
The short code a stock trades under, like ANT.

stories.headline: Nvidia doubles revenue to $115.8bn, but says Jensen Huang is not coming back
stories.dek: Board chair Harvey Jones shut the door on Huang's return on the company's first earnings call since his exit.
stories.caveman: Nvidia makes the chips that power most AI. On Tuesday it reported quarterly revenue of $115.84 billion, up 103% from a year ago and above Wall Street's guess of about $109 billion. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the former finance chief, presented the results. But the bigger headline: board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia 'does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.' Huang was pushed out over reported affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. Earlier the same day Huang said he would be 'honored' to return if asked, and he is due to testify to a House committee on Dec. 1. Nvidia stock rose about 5% after hours.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is Taiwan's biggest AI customer: TSMC, Foxconn and many others build its chips and servers. Its sales, and its leadership chaos, move Taiwan's stock market.
stories.camps: Some investors and tech leaders want Huang back, saying no one knows the company better. The board argues trust and national-security concerns make that impossible. Sales numbers suggest demand for AI chips is still very strong, for now.
stories.image_alt: Jensen Huang speaking in Taipei ahead of Computex, June 2024
stories.image_credit: Photo: Ann Wang/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: A company's official results for a three-month period: sales, profit and outlook.
A temporary boss while the company looks for a permanent one.
Buying and selling stocks after the main market closes.

stories.headline: Banks, flights, the NSA and Apple all crash in one week: US spy chief says it's not a cyberattack
stories.dek: Four major outages on four business days set off memes and conspiracy theories.
stories.caveman: In just a few days: Microsoft Outlook broke on Thursday, the FAA grounded flights on Friday, JPMorgan Chase and United Airlines had problems Monday, and on Tuesday the NSA's internal communications went down while Apple services like Apple Pay and iCloud stumbled. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC: 'This is not cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state.' Apple blamed an internal update and the NSA blamed scheduled maintenance. Security experts say companies are rushing to patch and upgrade old systems, partly with AI help, and stretched IT teams are making mistakes.
stories.why_it_matters: Everyday life now runs on a few giant tech systems. When one fails, payments, flights and messages stop for millions, including people in Taiwan who use the same services.
stories.camps: Officials and experts say it's an unlucky string of human and software errors. Some online think it's too many 'coincidences.' There is no public evidence of an attack, but the run of failures has raised questions about how fragile key systems are.
stories.image_alt: People walk past an Apple store
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: When a service or system stops working.
National Security Agency: the US spy agency for electronic communications.
A software fix for a bug or security hole.

stories.headline: California bans Waymo robotaxis from freeways after they drove into construction zones
stories.dek: The state calls the driverless cars an 'imminent hazard' after repeated incidents on Highway 101.
stories.caveman: Waymo, owned by Google's parent company Alphabet, runs the biggest fleet of driverless taxis in the US. California's Department of Motor Vehicles has now banned Waymo from operating or testing its driverless cars on all state freeways. Officials say three Waymo cars drove into an active construction closure south of San Francisco on Nov. 5, and another tried to get around highway patrol cars the next day; a video went viral. A similar incident happened in May. Waymo started driving on freeways around San Francisco, Los Angeles and Phoenix last year.
stories.why_it_matters: Self-driving cars are coming to more cities. This shows that regulators can, and will, pull them back when safety is in doubt, especially for workers on the road.
stories.camps: Safety officials and construction workers welcome the move. Waymo says the freeway incidents are being addressed and argues its cars are safer than human drivers overall. Robotaxi supporters fear heavy rules could slow a useful technology.
stories.image_alt: A Waymo vehicle on the freeway in Hawthorne, California
stories.image_credit: Photo: Mike Blake/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: A taxi that drives itself with no human driver.
Department of Motor Vehicles: the state office for driver licenses and vehicle rules.
A danger that could hurt people very soon.

stories.headline: Huang scandal gives Congress new energy to block AI chip sales to China
stories.dek: Both parties push to add tougher export rules to the must-pass defense bill in December.
stories.caveman: Revelations about Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy have revived efforts in Congress to cut off China from advanced AI chips. Lawmakers want to add several measures to the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), the yearly defense bill, due in December. Ideas include letting Congress review chip sales to rivals, having the Commerce Department track where advanced AI chips go, and blocking key chipmaking tools from going to China-linked firms. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Trump's administration has been 'completely disinterested in enforcing export controls.'
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan makes most advanced AI chips. New US rules decide who Taiwanese factories can sell to and how much paperwork every shipment needs.
stories.camps: Supporters, from both parties, say keeping AI chips from China protects US security and its tech lead. Critics, including many chip companies, say strict limits cost US firms sales and push China to build its own chips faster. The Trump administration has generally favored deals over tight controls.
stories.image_alt: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (file photo)
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: National Defense Authorization Act: the yearly US law that sets defense spending and policy.
Government rules that require permission to sell sensitive goods abroad.
Supported by both major parties.

stories.headline: Ukraine knocks out part of Putin's Crimean Bridge
stories.dek: A big arched section fell into the water after a missile-and-drone attack Zelensky called 'unprecedented.'
stories.caveman: The Crimean Bridge connects Russia to Crimea, the part of Ukraine Russia took in 2014. It carries roads and railways that bring Russian soldiers and supplies to the war. Putin himself opened it in 2018 by driving a truck across. Ukraine has hit it before, but this time cruise missiles and drones appear to have destroyed a large arched section of the road part. President Zelensky called it an 'unprecedented operation' weeks in the making. The Kremlin says it will rebuild the bridge 'better than before.' Meanwhile Russia keeps striking Kyiv, including bridges over the Dnipro River.
stories.why_it_matters: The bridge is both a supply line and a symbol. Damaging it makes it harder for Russia to keep troops in southern Ukraine supplied.
stories.camps: Many Ukrainians celebrated; some fear Russia will answer with even harder strikes on civilian power and infrastructure. Russia calls such attacks terrorism; Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate military target on its own land.
stories.image_alt: The damaged Crimean Bridge after the overnight attack
stories.image_credit: Image: BBC News

terms.explain: A peninsula in southern Ukraine that Russia annexed in 2014.
The seat of Russia's government; shorthand for Putin's administration.
A guided missile that flies low and far, like a small unmanned plane.

stories.headline: Trump lands in Manila on the way to a summit with Xi and Putin in China
stories.dek: He met Quad partners, signed a trade deal with Thailand, and heads next to Shenzhen for nuclear talks.
stories.caveman: President Trump arrived in the Philippines for a meeting of Southeast Asian leaders (Asean). He first met his 'Quad' partners: India's Narendra Modi, Japan's Sanae Takaichi and Australia's Anthony Albanese. He signed a trade deal with Thailand, which will drop tariffs on US goods. The US wants the region to join its 'Pax Silica' tech and AI network instead of China's. Next he flies to Shenzhen, China, for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders and nuclear talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. Asked whether Taiwan would come up with Xi, Trump said Xi would raise it.
stories.why_it_matters: Any US-China deal can touch Taiwan: chips, arms sales and how Washington talks about the island. Taiwan will be watching every word from Shenzhen.
stories.camps: Supporters say talking to rivals face to face lowers the risk of war. Critics worry Trump could trade away allies' interests, including Taiwan's, for a headline deal. Southeast Asian countries are still angry about tariffs and the Iran war's economic hit.
stories.image_alt: President Trump arrives in Manila
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via BBC News

terms.explain: Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a group of 11 regional countries.
A partnership of the US, Japan, India and Australia focused on the Indo-Pacific.
A US-led network of countries cooperating on chips, tech and AI supply chains.

stories.headline: Iran strikes Bahrain a third time; US hits back near the Strait of Hormuz
stories.dek: The tit-for-tat breaks a two-month lull in the Iran war, now in its eighth month.
stories.caveman: Bahrain, a small Gulf island country, hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet. On Tuesday Iran fired drones at a US radar site there, its third attack on American targets in Bahrain in five days. Bahrain says it shot them down, and the US says nothing was damaged and no one was hurt. Hours later a US fighter jet struck an Iranian Revolutionary Guard missile site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The US has blockaded Iran's ports for months, and the war that began Feb. 28 has disrupted the world's oil shipping. Trump has sent a third aircraft carrier to the region.
stories.why_it_matters: About a fifth of the world's oil passes the Strait of Hormuz. More fighting there means higher fuel and electricity prices, including in Taiwan.
stories.camps: The US says it is only answering Iranian 'aggression.' Iran says it is responding to the blockade that is choking its economy. Gulf neighbors condemned the attacks on Bahrain. Analysts warn stalled peace talks raise the risk of a much bigger escalation.
stories.image_alt: A woman holds an Iranian flag beneath a missile billboard in downtown Tehran
stories.image_credit: Photo: via NPR

terms.explain: A narrow sea passage off Iran that much of the world's oil passes through.
Using ships or forces to stop goods from going in or out of a country.
Iran's powerful elite military force, separate from the regular army.

stories.headline: Israel's parliament picks a speaker backed by Netanyahu's opponents
stories.dek: Matan Kahana won 66 of 120 votes, a key step toward a government without Netanyahu.
stories.caveman: The Knesset is Israel's parliament, with 120 seats. After the Oct. 27 election, Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies lost their majority. On Tuesday, after a stormy seven-hour debate, lawmakers elected Matan Kahana as speaker with 66 votes, backed by Jewish-led opposition parties and Arab-led parties. Netanyahu's candidate got 52. Kahana is an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief now trying to form a new government. Eisenkot's bloc has promised to undo some of Netanyahu's most contested policies.
stories.why_it_matters: Whoever leads Israel shapes the wars in Gaza and with Iran, and peace efforts in the Middle East.
stories.camps: Supporters call it a democratic turning point that reflects voters' wish for change. Netanyahu's camp says a coalition relying on Arab parties is fragile. Eisenkot still has to actually form a government, which could take weeks.
stories.image_alt: Matan Kahana, newly elected Knesset speaker
stories.image_credit: Photo: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: Israel's parliament.
The person who runs debates and votes in a parliament.
Several parties teaming up to reach a majority and form a government.

stories.headline: LeVar Burton's memoir: from almost-priest to Roots and Reading Rainbow
stories.dek: In 'Take My Word for It,' the Star Trek actor says he once dreamed of the priesthood, not TV.
stories.caveman: LeVar Burton grew up in Sacramento wanting to be a Catholic priest. Instead, as a college student, he landed the role of Kunta Kinte in the 1977 TV series Roots, about slavery in America. From 1983 to 2006 he hosted Reading Rainbow, a PBS kids' show built to get children excited about books over the summer. Many adults still tell him, sometimes in tears, what it meant to them. He also played Geordi La Forge on Star Trek: The Next Generation. His new memoir, Take My Word for It, looks back on all of it and on his late co-star Patrick Stewart.
stories.why_it_matters: Hot: a beloved reading champion writing his own story is exactly the kind of feel-good memoir that sells in the holiday season.
stories.camps: Fans love his warmth and his push for kids' reading. Some critics of celebrity memoirs find them light; NPR's interview suggests this one goes deeper into race and service.
stories.image_alt: LeVar Burton reads to students at a Chicago Public Library branch
stories.image_credit: Photo: via NPR

terms.explain: A book where a person tells their own life story.
A US kids' TV show (1983-2006) that encouraged reading.
A famous 1977 TV miniseries about an enslaved man and his descendants.

stories.headline: A novelist is on TIME's cover again: Caro Claire Burke
stories.dek: TIME's 100 must-read books of 2026 puts the 'Yesteryear' author front and center.
stories.caveman: TIME magazine released its list of 100 'must-read' books of 2026, and put novelist Caro Claire Burke, author of Yesteryear, on the cover. That is rare: Lit Hub notes the last novelist on TIME's cover was Taylor Jenkins Reid in 2025, and before that Akwaeke Emezi in 2021. Jonathan Franzen made headlines in 2010 as the first living novelist on the cover in a decade, and Colson Whitehead followed in 2019.
stories.why_it_matters: Who's hot: a magazine cover is a huge spotlight. It signals Burke is one of the year's breakout fiction writers.
stories.camps: Fans say it's great to see fiction get mainstream attention again. Skeptics note magazine lists are partly marketing and leave out many deserving books.
stories.image_alt: TIME magazine cover featuring Caro Claire Burke
stories.image_credit: Image: TIME cover via Literary Hub

terms.explain: The main article a magazine features on its front cover.
A curated list of books editors recommend.

stories.headline: Chad Harbach returns 15 years after 'The Art of Fielding' with 'The Brightness'
stories.dek: The Guardian calls the long-awaited sequel ambitious, but it will always be measured against the debut.
stories.caveman: In 2011 Chad Harbach's first novel, The Art of Fielding, was praised as a possible 'Great American Novel.' It is set at a small Midwestern college and full of baseball, ambition and failure; it sold for more than $650,000 after a bidding war. Harbach reportedly worked on it for over a decade. Now, 15 years later, comes the follow-up, The Brightness, returning to campus life. The Guardian review calls it an ambitious sequel, while noting any book this long-awaited will be read against the original.
stories.why_it_matters: Who's back: a much-hyped author's second act is one of the season's big literary events.
stories.camps: Admirers welcome his return to big American themes. Some reviewers wonder if any sequel can match the buzz of the first book.
stories.image_alt: Campus life, illustrating the setting of The Brightness
stories.image_credit: Photo: JasonDoiy/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: The idea of a book that captures the spirit of America.
A book that continues an earlier story.
A writer's first published book.

stories.headline: Big Tuesday for books: Shteyngart essays and a hidden DeLillo hockey novel
stories.dek: Gary Shteyngart's first essay collection lands alongside a reissue of Don DeLillo's secret novel.
stories.caveman: Tuesday is new-book day in the US. Lit Hub's list highlights Gary Shteyngart's first essay collection, The Sensualist, praised as 'hilarious and heartfelt'; Book V of Danish writer Solvej Balle's time-loop series On the Calculation of Volume; and a reissue of Amazons, a hockey romp Don DeLillo wrote under the fake name Cleo Birdwell. One blurb jokes that DeLillo foreshadowed 'hockey erotica.'
stories.why_it_matters: Who's hot: Shteyngart is a well-loved US comic writer, and a 'secret' DeLillo book is catnip for literary fans.
stories.camps: Book lists like this are recommendations, not reviews; tastes vary. Some purists find DeLillo's pseudonymous romp a curiosity rather than essential reading.
stories.image_alt: Book cover featured in Lit Hub's new releases list
stories.image_credit: Image: publisher cover via Literary Hub

terms.explain: A book of short nonfiction pieces.
A new printing of an older book.
A fake name an author writes under.

stories.headline: US loses its 'measles-free' status after 26 years
stories.dek: 5,400 cases and 10 deaths this year; Mexico and Bolivia also lost the status.
stories.caveman: Measles is a very contagious virus that causes a red rash and can kill or cause lasting harm, mostly in children. A vaccine (MMR) made it rare. The Pan American Health Organization, part of the UN system, says the same measles strain has spread non-stop in the US for more than 12 months, so the US is no longer counted as having 'eliminated' measles. The US has had about 5,400 cases and 10 deaths this year, the most since the 1990s. PAHO blamed 'gaps in vaccination.' The CDC says it wants to win the status back by expanding vaccine access.
stories.why_it_matters: Diseases cross borders on planes. Taiwan's CDC has raised its travel warning for the US and urges pregnant women and babies to avoid going.
stories.camps: Public health experts say falling vaccine rates and distrust are to blame. Some vaccine skeptics argue for personal choice. Doctors stress the vaccine is safe and the main way to stop outbreaks.
stories.image_alt: A health worker prepares a measles vaccine
stories.image_credit: Photo: via BBC News

terms.explain: A highly contagious virus that causes fever and a rash.
Official label that a disease no longer spreads continuously in a country.
The vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella.

stories.headline: Costa Rican journalist who exposed drug-gang ties is shot dead
stories.dek: Camilo Rodríguez had reported death threats; it may be the country's first journalist murder in over 20 years.
stories.caveman: Costa Rica has long been one of Central America's calmest countries. On Monday gunmen on a motorbike ambushed reporter Camilo Rodríguez, 50, in his car north of the capital, San José. He had spent decades in radio and print and recently posted videos naming judges, businesspeople and politicians he accused of corruption and links to drug traffickers. He had said he was getting death threats. The head of the journalists' association said 'all evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice.' International gangs are growing in Costa Rica and pushing up its murder rate.
stories.why_it_matters: When reporters are killed, people lose the truth about crime and corruption. A free press is part of what keeps any democracy honest, including Taiwan's.
stories.camps: Press groups call it an attack on free speech. Police have not yet named a motive or suspects. Some note his online accusations were not always verified, but that never justifies violence.
stories.image_alt: Police cordon off the scene of the shooting
stories.image_credit: Photo: via BBC News

terms.explain: Moving and selling illegal drugs, often by organized gangs.
The right of journalists to report without fear or censorship.
A surprise attack from a hidden position.

stories.headline: ICE agents pepper-spray a pregnant US citizen filming an arrest in California
stories.dek: Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23 and 12 weeks pregnant, was thrown to the ground outside a jail in Modesto.
stories.caveman: ICE is the US immigration enforcement agency. On Sunday, outside the Stanislaus county jail in Modesto, California, agents moved to arrest a man who appeared to have just been released. A group of locals who watch for ICE activity protested and filmed. Video shot by her husband shows Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, a 23-year-old US citizen who is 12 weeks pregnant, being pepper-sprayed, thrown down and arrested while lying on her stomach, according to her family's lawyer.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how tense immigration raids have become in the US, and how even citizens who watch or record can get hurt. Recording police is legal in the US.
stories.camps: Her supporters call it excessive force against a peaceful observer. Immigration officials often say protesters interfere with arrests and put agents at risk. The Guardian report did not include a detailed ICE response.
stories.image_alt: Still from video of ICE agents confronting protesters in Modesto
stories.image_credit: Image: video still via The Guardian

terms.explain: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which arrests and deports immigrants.
A spray that burns the eyes and skin, used to control people.
Police using more force than needed.

stories.headline: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead in West Bank village where settlers moved in
stories.dek: Palestinians blame settlers; the Israeli army describes a car-ramming and stone-throwing attack.
stories.caveman: The West Bank is Palestinian land Israel has occupied since 1967. Israeli 'settlers' are civilians who build or move into homes there, which most of the world considers illegal. In al-Duyuk al-Tahta near Jericho, settlers moved into eight houses on Nov. 4 after buying them in what they called a secretive operation. On Monday night a Palestinian woman in her 70s, Fadda al-Fahidat, was shot dead and others were hurt. Local Palestinians say settlers harassed them and opened fire. The Israeli army says a Palestinian car rammed an Israeli vehicle, rocks were thrown, and Israelis fired back; it did not mention her death. The same day the UK announced its first sanctions on firms working in the settlements.
stories.why_it_matters: Violence in the West Bank can spill into wider war and shapes how the world sees Israel's next government.
stories.camps: Accounts conflict sharply, and no independent investigation has reported yet. Palestinians and rights groups say settler violence is rising with little punishment. Israel's army says its people acted in self-defense.
stories.image_alt: Mourners at the funeral of Fadda al-Fahidat in al-Duyuk al-Tahta
stories.image_credit: Photo: via BBC News

terms.explain: Palestinian territory west of the Jordan River, occupied by Israel since 1967.
Israeli civilians living in communities built on occupied land.
Penalties like bans or frozen money to pressure a country, company or person.
